query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy-alloy-specific interatomic potential calibrated against first‐principles data can accurately and efficiently predict the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline high-entropy alloys (in near-equiatomic compositions) near their melting point
generation.intervention: Apply classical molecular dynamics simulations using the newly developed, tailored interatomic potential designed specifically for HEAs
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted under high-temperature conditions near the melting transition for alloys composed of five or more metallic elements (typically 5–35 at.% each)
generation.structural_mediator: The atomistic representation of multi-element interactions as captured by the specialized interatomic potential
generation.mechanism: The potential embeds first‐principles energy landscapes into a computationally efficient MD framework; this allows it to accurately model the disintegration of the crystalline phase and the associated enthalpic, entropic, and volumetric changes upon melting
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulated melting temperatures and fusion properties will agree with high-fidelity experimental measurements or first-principles benchmarks within an error margin of approximately 5–10%, and the computational time will be significantly lower compared to direct ab initio methods
generation.baseline: Conventional techniques such as differential scanning calorimetry and standard molecular dynamics with generic potentials either require extensive experimental runs or fail to capture the full thermodynamic picture across the vast composition space
generation.boundary: This method is expected to be robust for near-equiatomic HEAs with five or more elements; its applicability to non-equiatomic or heavily phase-separated alloys is uncertain and may require further refinement
generation.uncertainty: The exact error margins and transferability of the potential across all possible HEA compositions remain to be fully validated; performance under extreme compositional or temperature conditions is not yet established

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of high-entropy alloys spanning the equiatomic compositional space and perform both MD simulations using the new potential and high-precision experimental measurements (e.g., DSC, drop calorimetry). Compare the predicted melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, fusion entropies, volume changes at melting, and key liquid-phase properties with the experimental data.
measurements: Additional liquid-phase thermodynamic properties (such as heat capacity or viscosity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation results consistently deviate from the experimental measurements by more than approximately 10% or fail to capture qualitative trends in the phase transition, then the hypothesis that the specialized potential provides an accurate and efficient determination of HEA melting properties will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. frame.goal: To develop an approach that accurately and efficiently determines melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of high-entropy alloy compositions.
frame.limitation: Existing approaches may be too time-consuming, computationally expensive, or not generally applicable to the vast compositional space of high-entropy alloys, lacking in both accuracy and efficiency.
